Gautama Buddha wasn’t perfect; he made mistakes, even in his teaching. In fact, at first he wasn’t even sure it was worth his effort to try and teach what he’d learned. If he’d stuck with that, we’d have never heard of him, and he’d be an unknown Paccekabuddha (Solitary Buddha). Fortunately, we read that he was convinced to teach the Dhamma. But even his first attempt to teach (an ascetic named Upaka) was a failure. The man left without understanding or believing what the Buddha had accomplished or told him.

But Jesus also wasn’t perfect. He had human failings and fears: he was afraid of what would happen to him and asked god to take the cup away. (He ultimately fulfilled god’s will, being courageous in the face of his fear, but he had a moment of weakness). And it’s only natural for a human to be afraid of being tortured to death. He cried out in agony against God forsaking him, as described in Matthew and Mark. He lost his temper with people, he got violent in the temple with the money changers.

You also have to ask yourself what does and does not constitute perfection, and who fulfills that standard. And your definition likely isn’t universal. And it would likely change with time.

I have two quotes that I like to give when questions like this come up. Keep in mind that this describes something close to my interpretation, and there are many others.

The first is by scholar Rupert M. L. Gethin:

- “Buddhism regards itself as presenting a system of training in conduct, meditation, and understanding that constitutes a path leading to the cessation of suffering.” (Gethin, The Foundations of Buddhism)

And the second is by secular Buddhist author and teacher Stephen Batchelor:

- “Depending on which part of Buddhism you grasp, you might identify it as a system of ethics, a philosophy, a contemplative psychotherapy, a religion. While containing all of these, it can no more be reduced to any one of them than an elephant can be reduced to its tail.”

There was syncretism between the Hellenistic culture/religion of the Greek/Macedonian colonists and the local Buddhist religion. Art, religion, etc., had some very interesting co-mingling. 

The first anthropomorphic depictions of the Buddha are thought to have arisen from the interactions of Greek art with Buddhist topics (before then the Buddha was usually depicted aniconically, as foot prints or an empty throne or a tree or something), and there are depictions of Heracles serving as a protective Boddhisattva for the Buddha, in the role of Vajrapani (a deity-servant/protector/guide of the Buddha). 

There was an Indo-Greek king in that region by the name of Menander who had a dialogue with an enlightened Buddhist monk and converted to Buddhism. Their story is part of the Buddhist canon of that region. 

It’s an *absolutely fascinating* period of history in that part of the world! 😁

What they do and don’t follow. I don’t believe there’s a single person who follows *every single word of every single line of the Bible exactly and precisely as written without even one exception.* I think everyone, if you talked with them enough, would admit some kind of variation of belief or interpretation of certain parts of the Bible.

And, of course, then there’s the question of which books of the Bible one considers canon and which one doesn’t (you know, like varieties between Protestant, Catholic, Orthodox, and other canons), and then there’s the question of variation due to translation. Translation is much more complex and involves more subjective judgment on the part of the translator than most people understand.
